h: A Stradivarius, the Alfred Jewel and lunch on the roof
p: Some of the Ashmolean's treasures have stories that could fill a book. The Alfred Jewel, a gold and enamel object found in Somerset in the 17th century, carries an inscription that translates as 'Alfred ordered me to be made', linking it to Alfred the Great. Nobody is completely sure what it was used for, which only adds to its charm. Nearby, Powhatan's Mantle, a deerskin decorated with shells, is one of the most important surviving objects from early contact between English settlers and Native Americans.

Music lovers should look for the Messiah Stradivarius, a violin made by Antonio Stradivari in 1716 and kept in remarkably fresh condition, as it has hardly ever been played. Over in the painting galleries, Paolo Uccello's The Hunt in the Forest draws you deep into a dark woodland full of riders and hounds. There's also plenty from ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and a remarkable collection relating to the Minoan civilisation of Crete.

The museum was transformed in 2009 with a bright modern extension behind the old façade, so the galleries feel airy and easy to explore. Entry to the main collection is free, which means you can dip in for an hour or spend most of the day. Up top, the rooftop restaurant offers lovely views across Oxford's rooftops and spires.

Afterwards, Oxford has plenty more to enjoy on foot. The Pitt Rivers Museum and the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, sharing a building just to the north, are wonderfully eccentric, while the Covered Market is ideal for a bite and a browse.
